agents.name: Codex

surface_source.quote: my tendency has been to type to agents in a CLI

agents.quote: Just like with Google Docs, I consider codex above average in terms of software quality in the space, but even though I haven't been using it for a year, I could easily write 10k words on all the workarounds I've implemented (either by habit or, in some cases, with actual scripts that monitor for broken behavior and then correct it).

also.quote: With a semi-autonomous workflow, I can exhaust a week's quota on the $200/mo codex plan in ~10 minutes of my time.

history.quote: I'm sort of in the stone ages with my setup (codex plugin in vscode).

models.name: GPT-5.6 Sol
models.quote: Since my original goal here was to see what happens when you run a current (public) SOTA agent in a loop (GPT-5.6 Sol) without much supervision on a non-trivial code optimization problem without any real supervision

also.quote: In the same way that I don't prompt GPT-5.6 the same way I prompted GPT-5.5, I don't think I'd want to use the same skills.

history.quote: I used GPT-5.2 (seems to give you the most quota, and I did this in a way that used a ton of quota; even on the Pro plan, I had to throttle my usage) to generate code which ran on my laptop.
To start with, I'd been using a lot of GPT-5.5 xhigh when this discussion came up a couple months ago and I benchmarked this thing

review_style.value: Heavy randomized testing instead of human review
review_style.quote: Personally, I'm very comfortable shipping code without human review because I've seen it done on products that are technically more challenging than most software at most software companies.

also.quote: Personally, I think this can be effective enough that I'm fairly comfortable trying to ship a large volume of code via a "software factories" workflow because I've seen a testing-heavy no-review workflow that results in much higher quality than any review-reliant workflow I've seen or even heard of.
If you have the budget, false positive rejection is straightforward (ask agent to repro, have agents independently check if the repro is valid).

harness.value: One-off agent-written loop scripts with health checks, on laptops and AWS hosts
harness.quote: As a result, what I've ended up doing is making one-off loops for tasks that need to run for a while.

also.quote: In that era, I think I was just managing GPT "manually" by having it build map-reduce-like graphs of what I wanted to do, custom for each problem.

history.value: Queued copies of one prompt in the Codex VS Code plugin
history.quote: I wouldn't recommend anyone use this because the plugin is so buggy, but it works ok enough if you want to queue up a bunch of work and occasionally check in on what it's doing.

parallelism.quote: Just for example, one that I've seen come up repeatedly related to the earlier note that, on tasks that I do, adding a clear, strict, instruction in AGENTS.md to not do something fails once every week or two when juggling 10 agents, a failure rate of something like one per 100 rule-agent-days.

rules_files.quote: When I offhandedly mentioned this to Yossi Kreinin, he suggested adding a note at the bottom of my AGENTS.md to re-read instruction after compaction.

signature.caption: with contrarian personas
signature.why: Our pick: instead of switching models, he has independent agents review as named engineers (and as himself) plus contrarians, which he says beat the same token budget spent otherwise.
signature.quote: so I tried diagnosing issues with something like "use independent agents to review as linus torvalds, kyle kingsbury, marc brooker, tptacek, dan luu, and 4 contrarian personas. have each think for a long time", with multiple iterations of this (yes, I do find it quite silly to invoke my own name).

archetype.why: Skips off-the-shelf orchestrators and has Codex build custom loops and map-reduce graphs per problem, checked by tests rather than review.

signature_quote.value: When I use LLMs I'm generally trying to get as much work as possible out of a unit of my time.
signature_quote.more: I often want to type for a few minutes to get something to loop for hours to days.
